narrative.text: The back cover (in Arabic) of WHO's guidance on preparing for the introduction of HPV vaccines, giving contact details for the Department of Reproductive Health and Research and listing contributing WHO departments and UNFPA. The contact details and Latin-script addresses were extracted as garbled, reversed characters.
A list of additional resources (in Arabic) from UNFPA, WHO, the Global Immunization Vision and Strategy and GAVI; the web addresses were extracted as garbled characters.
The title page (in Arabic) of the guidance on preparing for the introduction of HPV vaccines: policy and programme guidance for countries.

The copyright and disclaimer page (in Arabic) of the HPV vaccine introduction guidance, dated 2006, with WHO publication contact details and a note that it reflects the views of an international expert group; parts of the contact details are garbled.

The table of contents (in Arabic) of the HPV vaccine guidance, listing sections on cervical cancer and HPV, the vaccines, target populations, introduction challenges, advocacy, service delivery, partnerships, monitoring and financing.

Acknowledgements (in Arabic) explaining that the guidance draws on a technical consultation on sexual and reproductive health programmes and HPV vaccines held in Montreux in March 2006. It lists the expert participants and the contributing WHO departments.

Introduces the HPV vaccine guidance (in Arabic), prepared after the joint UNFPA–WHO consultation to alert stakeholders in sexual and reproductive health, immunization, adolescent health and cancer control to issues around the imminent introduction of HPV vaccines. It describes the burden of cervical cancer and notes that cytology-based screening has sharply reduced deaths in high-income countries.

Summarises World Health Assembly resolution WHA58.22 (2005) on cancer prevention and control, which links cervical cancer control to reproductive health goals (in Arabic). A chart on HPV infection, precancerous lesions and cancer by age is included, with its source citation extracted as garbled text.

Describes visual inspection with acetic acid and cryotherapy as a simpler screening and treatment approach for low-resource settings, whose impact still needs study (in Arabic). A chart of cervical cancer incidence by region follows, with a garbled source citation.

Describes the two HPV vaccines, which target types 16 and 18 that cause most cervical cancers, one also covering types causing genital warts (in Arabic). It reports near-complete protection against precancerous lesions in trials and the expected registration timelines of Gardasil and Cervarix.

Explains that HPV vaccines are expected to be licensed first for girls and young women, with stronger immune responses in young adolescents than older girls (in Arabic). It notes unknowns such as safety in pregnancy and the value of vaccinating older or previously infected women.

Describes innovative features of HPV vaccines in relation to WHO's global reproductive health strategy and its five core elements (in Arabic). It contrasts HPV vaccines with hepatitis B vaccine, which is given to infants and needed no direct link to cancer control programmes.

Describes the WHO–UNICEF Global Immunization Vision and Strategy and its goals for wider, equitable immunization (in Arabic). It notes that HPV vaccine introduction can strengthen cervical cancer prevention and may offer lessons for a future HIV vaccine.

Links HPV vaccines to HIV and sexual and reproductive health agendas and WHO's global STI strategy (in Arabic). It warns that high vaccine cost could limit access and calls for public–private partnerships, then begins discussing country-specific challenges of introduction.

Notes that vaccinating young girls against an STI-related disease is sensitive in some settings and that complementary messages on delaying sexual debut, condom use and screening must be preserved (in Arabic). It calls for updated national cervical cancer strategies and international partnerships to speed availability and affordable prices in developing countries.

Describes challenges in advocacy, information and communication on HPV vaccines for different audiences, including balancing information on benefits and limits (in Arabic). It lists key messages, such as the expected protection against most cervical cancers and the greater impact of vaccination before sexual debut.

Continues the key messages (in Arabic): HPV vaccines may also protect against vulvar and vaginal cancers and warts but not other STIs or HIV, and screening must continue because some cancers are not prevented. It advises that health promotion be based on country contexts and that countries adapt UNFPA and WHO materials.

Sets out messages for key audiences such as national policy-makers, programme managers and service providers, including coordination with screening programmes (in Arabic). It suggests using HPV vaccination to strengthen existing adolescent programmes such as school health initiatives.

Discusses reaching the target population (in Arabic), likely girls aged about 9 to 13 before sexual debut, with a separate catch-up group. It considers school-based delivery, community adolescent programmes and the limits of such programmes for reaching out-of-school youth.

Continues on service delivery (in Arabic), suggesting referral mechanisms such as vaccine vouchers and roles for civil society in reaching out-of-school youth. It discusses the catch-up population and stresses that vaccinated women and those too old for vaccination should still be screened according to national guidelines.

Stresses that HPV vaccination should be part of comprehensive, rights-based services rather than a stand-alone strategy, building on existing structures such as the cold chain (in Arabic). It describes monitoring and evaluation, including use of precancerous lesions as markers and post-marketing surveillance where cancer registries are weak.

Lists in Arabic the action points for HPV vaccine service delivery in WHO/UNFPA guidance on preparing to introduce HPV vaccines, such as linking stakeholders, defining the main target group, overcoming sociocultural barriers and checking school enrolment of 9–13-year-olds. It also calls for a delivery strategy that extends immunization services beyond infants, consistent messaging and health worker training, alongside comprehensive cervical cancer prevention with screening, treatment and monitoring of vaccine impact.

Discusses in Arabic stewardship and financing for HPV vaccine introduction, urging that mobilising resources be a high priority within broader partner strategies and health system strengthening. It notes the challenges of vaccine cost and competing priorities, the value of lessons from hepatitis B vaccine introduction, and the need for epidemiological data, demand forecasting and cost analyses. It stresses securing international funding commitments, for example through GAVI, UNICEF and the PAHO Revolving Fund.

Explains in Arabic that international funding commitments would encourage manufacturers to expand supply and help secure negotiated prices for low-resource settings, and that without them countries must rely on public resources, donations or private-sector introduction. It advises aligning HPV vaccine planning with multi-year immunization and sector-wide plans, linking with GAVI applications, and setting oversight conditions for private-sector introduction, before listing action points such as forming a national HPV vaccine working group.

Continues in Arabic the financing action points, calling for country-level demand forecasting and business cases using cervical and other anogenital cancer burden and HPV type data, involvement of reproductive health programmes in GAVI applications, and WHO/UNFPA technical help for countries not eligible for GAVI.

The Arabic conclusion of the HPV vaccine guidance, stating that introduction decisions rest with each country, that the vaccine should sit within integrated services and partnerships, and that equity concerns must be addressed so poorer women are reached. A box notes the June 2006 US FDA licensing of the quadrivalent HPV vaccine for girls and women aged 9–26 and the conditions it prevents.
A list in Arabic of additional resources, naming UNFPA, WHO, the Global Immunization Vision and Strategy and GAVI with web addresses that are garbled in the extracted text.
The Arabic back cover, giving WHO Department of Reproductive Health and Research contact details (partly garbled) and listing UNFPA and the WHO departments that prepared the HPV vaccine guidance.
